questions.q: Define import substitution strategy and name the two specific policy instruments used to implement it in India during 1950-1990.
questions.a: Import substitution is an inward-looking trade strategy that aims to replace imports with domestic production by protecting domestic industries from foreign competition. The two instruments are: (1) Tariffs - taxes on imported goods that raise their price, and (2) Quotas - quantitative limits on the volume of goods that can be imported. A wrong answer that only mentions "restrictions" without distinguishing tariffs (price-based) from quotas (quantity-based) reveals the student cannot differentiate between price and quantity instruments of trade policy.

questions.q: Why did India's planners choose import substitution over export promotion in the first seven Five Year Plans? Explain using the concepts of infant industry argument and foreign exchange scarcity.
questions.a: Planners chose import substitution because: (1) Infant industry argument - domestic industries were too young and inefficient to compete with established foreign producers; protection gave them time to achieve economies of scale and learn-by-doing. (2) Foreign exchange scarcity - India feared that free imports would drain limited foreign reserves on luxury/consumer goods rather than essential capital goods. A wrong answer that says "India wanted to be self-sufficient" without explaining the economic mechanism (infant industry learning + forex constraint) shows superficial understanding of the strategic rationale.

questions.q: Suppose India imposes a 50% tariff on imported cars. The world price of a car is ₹10 lakh. Domestic producers previously sold at ₹12 lakh but now face the tariff-inclusive import price. Calculate the new effective price of imported cars and explain whether domestic producers will necessarily raise their price to ₹15 lakh.
questions.a: Step 1: World price = ₹10 lakh. Step 2: Tariff = 50% of ₹10 lakh = ₹5 lakh. Step 3: New import price = ₹10 lakh + ₹5 lakh = ₹15 lakh. Step 4: Domestic producers need NOT raise price to ₹15 lakh; they can price anywhere below ₹15 lakh (e.g., ₹13 lakh) to capture market share while earning higher margins than before. Step 5: The tariff creates a "price ceiling" for domestic pricing, not a mandate. A wrong answer stating domestic price must equal ₹15 lakh reveals confusion between tariff-inclusive import price and domestic pricing strategy.

questions.q: Analyze how import substitution affected the following three variables in India during 1950-1990: (a) Industrial sector's share in GDP, (b) Variety of industries, (c) Quality of goods available to consumers. Use data from the NCERT text to support your analysis.
questions.a: (a) Industrial share in GDP rose from 13% (1950-51) to 24.6% (1990-91) - positive structural change. (b) Industry diversified beyond cotton textiles and jute into electronics, automobiles, heavy machinery - positive diversification. (c) Quality suffered because protection created captive markets; producers had no incentive to improve quality when consumers had no alternatives - negative welfare outcome. A wrong answer claiming all three improved shows inability to distinguish between quantitative growth (output/GDP share) and qualitative outcomes (consumer welfare, efficiency).

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Import substitution successfully achieved self-reliance in industrial production but failed to create internationally competitive industries." Provide two pieces of evidence supporting and two contradicting this view.
questions.a: Supporting: (1) India achieved self-sufficiency in many capital goods and intermediate goods previously imported. (2) Industrial base diversified significantly - public sector built heavy industries (steel, machinery) that private sector couldn't. Contradicting: (1) Protection continued long after industries matured (e.g., automobiles, electronics), leading to obsolete technology and high costs. (2) Export orientation was neglected until mid-1980s; India's share in world trade fell from 2.5% (1950) to 0.5% (1990). A wrong answer that only lists successes reveals confirmation bias and inability to weigh trade-offs between self-reliance and competitiveness.

questions.q: Design a trade policy for a hypothetical developing country in 2025 that wants to build a domestic solar panel industry. Specify: (a) Tariff rate and quota level, (b) Sunset clause (when protection ends), (c) Performance benchmark for domestic firms to qualify for continued protection. Justify each element.
questions.a: Good answer includes: (a) Tariff: 20-30% (not prohibitive), Quota: 30% of domestic demand (allows some competition). (b) Sunset clause: 7-10 years with mid-term review. (c) Benchmark: Domestic firms must achieve 80% of world-price efficiency and export 15% of output by year 5. Justification: Moderate protection balances infant industry learning with competitive pressure; sunset clause prevents permanent protection; export benchmark forces global competitiveness. A poor answer with 100% tariff, no sunset clause, and no benchmarks reveals failure to learn from India's experience of protection becoming permanent and anti-competitive.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Import substitution?
questions.a: Students often believe import substitution means "zero imports" or "complete ban on foreign goods." In reality, India never banned all imports; tariffs made imports expensive but not impossible, and quotas allowed limited quantities.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain how tariffs and quotas function as protectionist tools, analyze the rationale for import substitution in India's 1950-1990 context, and evaluate its impact on industrial diversification, consumer welfare, and export orientation using specific economic reasoning.
